metadata.title: Local Ranking Problem on the BrowseGraph

extraction_notes.note: The paper's findings are empirical observations read off tables and figures; the key ones are emitted as claim nodes with rigor numerical, while the tables and figures themselves (only in floats/images) are not nodes.

pseudocode_steps mis-parsed algorithm2e's two-body \eIf: it truncated the \For/\eIf step statements (ASP5, ASP7, ASP9) after the then-branch and parented the else-branch lines to ASP7. Overriding 'keep as returned', the three statements were re-sliced verbatim to their matching closing braces and the else-branch lines reparented to ASP9.
Dropped the comment-only pseudocode line (/* For each step ... */) and the trailing caption fragment after \Return as non-operations; steps renumbered.
LRP is stated both in the Introduction and in Related Work (Chen et al.); the Introduction's two-sentence formulation was kept as the single node.
theorem or remark: Bressan and Pretto's impossibility result is only summarized in words, but it is a cited result stated in full, so it is an external theorem.

sec:subgraphs.section: Subgraphs Based on Session Referrer URL

nodes.statement: More recently, centrality metrics have been applied to browsing graphs, (also referred to as BrowseGraphs\ ) where nodes are webpages and edges represent the transitions made by the users who navigate the links between them.
nodes.raw_latex: More recently, centrality metrics have been applied to \emph{browsing graphs}, (also referred to as \textit{BrowseGraphs}\ \cite{Liu2008a,trevisiol12image,TrevisiolRecSys14}) where nodes are webpages and edges represent the transitions made by the users who navigate the links between them.
nodes.clean_text: More recently, centrality metrics have been applied to browsing graphs, (also referred to as BrowseGraphs\ ) where nodes are webpages and edges represent the transitions made by the users who navigate the links between them.

nodes.statement: Comparative studies have shown that centrality-based algorithms applied over BrowseGraphs\ provide higher-quality rankings compared to standard hyperlink graphs.
conclusions: Comparative studies have shown that centrality-based algorithms applied over BrowseGraphs\ provide higher-quality rankings compared to standard hyperlink graphs.
nodes.raw_latex: Comparative studies have shown that centrality-based algorithms applied over \textit{BrowseGraphs}\ provide higher-quality rankings compared to standard hyperlink graphs~\cite{Liu2009, Liu2008a}.
nodes.clean_text: Comparative studies have shown that centrality-based algorithms applied over BrowseGraphs\ provide higher-quality rankings compared to standard hyperlink graphs.

nodes.statement: Bressan and Pretto proved that, in the general case, an efficient local ranking algorithm does not exist, and in order to compute a correct ranking it is necessary to visit at least a number of nodes linear in the size of the input graph.
conclusions: Bressan and Pretto proved that, in the general case, an efficient local ranking algorithm does not exist, and in order to compute a correct ranking it is necessary to visit at least a number of nodes linear in the size of the input graph.

nodes.clean_text: Bressan and Pretto proved that, in the general case, an efficient local ranking algorithm does not exist, and in order to compute a correct ranking it is necessary to visit at least a number of nodes linear in the size of the input graph.

nodes.statement: In this section we describe some analysis on these ReferrerGraphs, proving that they are consistently different not only in term of nodes and content but also in term of navigation patterns of the users.
nodes.raw_latex:
In this section we describe some analysis on these \textit{ReferrerGraphs}, proving that they are consistently different not only in term of nodes and content
but also in term of navigation patterns of the users.
nodes.clean_text: In this section we describe some analysis on these ReferrerGraphs, proving that they are consistently different not only in term of nodes and content but also in term of navigation patterns of the users.

nodes.statement: When the ranking between two subgraphs differs greatly (i.e., low Kendall's tau), it is an indication that they either show different content (i.e., webpages) or that the collective browsing behaviour in the two graphs privileged different sets of pages.
nodes.raw_latex: When the ranking between two subgraphs differs greatly (\emph{i.e.}, low Kendall's $\tau$), it is an indication that they either show different content (\emph{i.e.}, webpages) or that the collective browsing behaviour in the two graphs privileged different sets of pages.
nodes.clean_text: When the ranking between two subgraphs differs greatly (i.e., low Kendall's tau), it is an indication that they either show different content (i.e., webpages) or that the collective browsing behaviour in the two graphs privileged different sets of pages.

nodes.statement: In S we showed how users coming from different sources (i.e., referrer domains) behave differently in terms of content discovery and, as a consequence, the importance of the news articles vary significantly among the different BrowseGraphs.

nodes.statement: For each subgraph G_i, we simulated a random surfer moving around in G_i (i.e., calling the function RandomSurfer(i, alpha, steps, G)), computing at each step (i.e., page visited) the probability of the surfer to navigate in each subgraph G_1, dots G_7: we expect that the probability corresponding to G_i will increase at each step, and will eventually dominate all the others.

eventually dominate all the others.
